talks.title: Hardware Hacking all the things, on a budget - You can do it too!
talks.teaser: Shows how to tear down cheap devices, locate test points and dump firmware with affordable tools and no soldering.
talks.summary:
The talk makes the case that hardware hacking is an accessible hobby that does not require expensive gear or soldering skills. The speaker, a red teamer, starts with how consumer electronics are manufactured, from bare boards through component placement and test stations. Test points and leftover secrets often survive into shipped products, and a factory story about faulty flash chips in network equipment shows why that matters.

The middle section covers reconnaissance and tooling. Useful starting points include companion apps and web interfaces, firmware downloads, teardowns, open-source router projects that document debug pads, and FCC filings that contain internal photos and frequency details. Budget equipment such as spring-loaded test probes, clips and a cheap logic analyzer that decodes serial traffic lets a beginner reach a board's UART without soldering. A low-cost Nordic development kit is presented as a training board, where the speaker compiles and flashes a small program, reads memory, dumps firmware and single-steps code over the debug interface.

The demonstrations include a router used by a Finnish ISP, where a serial port was found, the bootloader and web firmware were extracted, and the device was shown to be a working Linux system. A returned-goods device bought at a discount store was opened in the same way to reach a shell. The closing advice is to buy spare units before experimenting, check ground and power wiring on cheap tools, disable unused external interfaces, avoid storing secrets on devices, and ask questions in the hardware community.

talks.title: How CSPM Can Help to Secure Your Cloud and Avoid Configuration Disasters
talks.teaser: Shows how cloud security posture management finds infrastructure misconfigurations that application scans miss, and how to triage them.
talks.summary:
Mikael Nilsson opens with the case for cloud security posture management (CSPM). He cites Verizon's 2023 breach report and the OWASP Top 10 to show how often misconfigurations appear in breaches. He then walks through an application that passes static, dynamic, composition and container scans, yet still leaks data through an open storage bucket, an exposed database or an overly broad dataset. CSPM targets that infrastructure layer surrounding the code.

The middle of the talk covers organisation and process. Product security and cloud infrastructure teams have traditionally owned different halves of security, and infrastructure as code means developers now share responsibility for what they deploy. CSPM tools evaluate cloud resources against framework, regulatory and internal policy rules, then track findings over time. Nilsson recommends choosing a few frameworks, such as ISO 27001, SOC 2, NIST CSF, GDPR or CIS benchmarks, instead of starting with everything. His triage approach sorts findings into quick switch-flips, high-effort changes that need planning or compensating controls, and high-volume or regressing issues that point to broken controls. He also shows posture scores and severity trends as progress measures, and a cloned load balancer rule that enforces an internal TLS 1.3 policy.

He closes by urging regular meetings between developers and operations, and by pairing standard benchmarks with custom rules for enterprise policy. The examples use mock data from one commercial CSPM product, presented as one option among many.

talks.title: Hacking Hearts and Minds
talks.teaser: Shows how communication, storytelling and influence skills can help security staff win support without formal authority.
talks.summary:
The talk argues that social skills and communication are abilities people can practice and improve over time, not traits reserved for a lucky few. The speaker, a security leader who moved from developer to CISO, describes how becoming a parent prompted him to rethink his career, and how a book on influence without authority pushed him to focus on persuading people he did not manage.

He then covers the experience that shaped his approach. Giving talks helped him structure ideas and practice public speaking, and mentors taught him how to pitch to executives in the short time they allow. Reviewing many team security self-assessments taught him to read rooms, adapt to different audiences and handle first impressions. He also explains how a gap between self-perception and how colleagues see you can weaken your credibility, using his own reputation as a joker as an example, and suggests building enough trust to ask for honest feedback.

The later sections turn to practical techniques. Storytelling can make security numbers and incidents compelling, and explanations should be adapted for executives versus developers. He describes lobbying by meeting each decision-maker one-on-one before a key meeting, seizing openings after incidents to win budget, and using body language and mirroring to build rapport. The takeaway is to treat communication as a deliberate skill and to use influence to get security prioritized.

talks.title: How Much Dirty Laundry Are Your Smart Home Devices Airing About You
talks.teaser: Shows how much personal data two smartwatches send to their makers, and how to limit it.
talks.summary:
The talk asks how much personal data connected devices send back to their manufacturers. The speaker, a security consultant with a privacy interest, first planned to study a smart washing machine and a robot vacuum, but after the vacuum failed he switched to two smartwatches: a Samsung Galaxy Watch 4 and a Garmin Forerunner 245. He opened with context on how sensitive wearable health data is and past cases where location data from fitness devices exposed people.

The method moved from simple checks to deeper ones. He read the privacy policies, compared the permissions each Android app requested, and looked up third-party trackers with an online database. He then decompiled the app packages and searched them for partner and third-party references. Finally, he routed app traffic through a web proxy on a rooted phone with a trusted certificate, and logged DNS lookups through a filtering service. Garmin traffic was largely readable and mapped to upload, weight and gear services. Samsung traffic was mostly encrypted, and his decryption attempts did not succeed. He also noted that a Samsung voice assistant consent could extend to other devices on the account.

The takeaways were practical. Blocking third-party domains through DNS can reduce tracking, but blocking vendor domains leaves the watch close to useless. Garmin devices can work without the companion app, while the Samsung model needed its phone app. Some devices can be moved to an open-source replacement backend. His advice was to weigh features against data collection, turn off tracking that is not needed, and read privacy policies closely.

talks.title: Weaponizing Plain Text ANSI Escape Sequences as a Forensic Nightmare
talks.teaser: Shows how crafted ANSI escape sequences hidden in log files can deceive analysts and, in some terminals, run commands.
talks.summary:
The talk opens with an incident responder who exports a large log file and opens it in a terminal, only to find a ransom-style message and a payload that launches a calculator. The speaker explains that terminal control codes, the escape sequences that set colors and move the cursor, are what make such content render and act on screen. Starting from a Rack advisory about shell escape injection through logging middleware, the research set out to turn log entries into command execution.

Testing compared how shells, editors, browsers and command-line tools such as cat, less and curl display these codes, and how attacker-controlled text reaches logs through HTTP requests, Docker output and DNS records. Early published vectors, including old title-setting and report-back sequences, had already been fixed, so attention moved to hyperlinks, clipboard writes, inline images, cursor movement, printer triggers and mouse reporting. These produced spoofing, hidden content and denial of service in several terminals. Command execution came from terminal query responses, extending earlier work by David Leadbeater, and from file transfer prompts and an editor's rerun-command feature.

Vendor responses varied: GitHub limited colors to a safe subset, Kibana needed several fixes and Splunk reworked parts of its system. The main takeaway is that log files are untrusted input. Sanitize data before it is written, escape it before display, and remember that responders reading logs in a terminal are themselves a target.

talks.title: Creating Monsters
talks.teaser: Walks through maintaining the ffuf web fuzzer, from community growth and feature requests to rejecting pull requests.
talks.summary:
The speaker, who leads security testing at a company and maintains the ffuf web fuzzer, starts by contrasting offensive tooling that often breaks with the stable, predictable software he wanted. The project began when an existing tool's maintainers asked contributors to pause during a large refactor, so the feature he needed was built independently. Early growth came from conference talks and social media, and the design choices were shaped by open discussion with a growing community.

The middle of the talk looks at the less pleasant side of maintenance. Clear bug reports, documentation and tutorials help the project, while vague reports, repeated basic questions and entitlement consume time. Rejecting well-meant pull requests that clash with the tool's vision is described as the hardest part, although one persistent contributor changed his mind about automatic CSRF token handling. He also raises the tool's misuse in a government report about attacks on Ukrainian targets, which he says raises ethical questions he cannot answer neatly.

Finally, he notes that open-source maintenance rarely pays a living, with sponsorship income small and a one-year sponsorship from a training provider a notable exception. His takeaways are to hold a shared vision, communicate it openly, stay objective toward contributors, be kind, and maintain projects out of passion rather than for money.

talks.title: I'm a script kiddie, bypassing your antivirus and EDR systems
talks.teaser: Explains how DLL side-loading through vulnerable applications can slip past antivirus and EDR, shown with a Bitwarden demo.

talks.title: Smoke and Mirrors: How to hide in Microsoft Azure
talks.teaser: Shows how Microsoft Entra enumeration can avoid Graph activity logs, and how Azure ML exposes stored credentials.
talks.summary:
The speakers, both from With Secure, open by arguing that attackers are moving toward cloud services. They cite Microsoft's 2023 Digital Defense Report and the large volume of password spraying against Microsoft accounts. Microsoft Entra is presented as the core identity platform behind Microsoft 365 and Azure, which makes it a high-value target. They note that the new Microsoft Graph activity logs help, but do not cover everything.

The middle of the talk compares several ways of querying Entra. Listing conditional access policies through the Graph API produces a Graph activity log entry. The same request made through the legacy Azure AD Graph, the internal IAM API used by the portal, or the provisioning and app management APIs was not logged in the places they checked. The speakers explain that first-party pre-consented clients sidestep the usual admin consent requirement, and that common offensive and defensive tools rely on them. They then move to Azure Machine Learning. In a demo, a low-privileged reader used the workspace datastore pages to retrieve storage account keys and a SQL service principal secret. That principal could then read a Key Vault secret the reader could not access directly.

The closing advice is to restrict which clients can sign in, using app assignment or conditional access. Teams should prefer identity-based access over credential-based access so permissions remain auditable. Logs from several services should be combined into one analysis platform, and controls should be reassessed regularly because provider behaviour changes.

talks.title: Circling Dragons: Red Team Lessons From Modern Breaches
talks.teaser: Reviews public breach reports from an attacker's viewpoint and draws red team lessons on pacing, social engineering and tradecraft.
talks.summary:
Jason Lang, a red team practice lead, reads public breach reports from the attacker's side rather than the defender's. He argues that breach write-ups often describe intrusions as sophisticated to make the victim look less negligent, and he sorts the cases he reviewed into novice, professional and nation-state groups.

The novice case was a database server exposed to the internet, brute-forced and followed by ransomware in under an hour. The professional cases included a Caesars intrusion tied to Scattered Spider, where help desk social engineering and identity infrastructure played a role, and a cloud company breach where the intruder read internal documentation, planted persistence and was caught after escalating too quickly. The nation-state examples involved zero-day exploitation of email gateways and firewall management tools, with attackers living inside network devices rather than relying on common Active Directory techniques.

For practitioners, Lang's takeaways are to scale the attack to the target's maturity, monitor before acting, slowly work existing access and internal applications, keep backup access in place, and aim for the effect rather than copying a specific exploit. He also argues that phone-based social engineering is often the most effective first step, and that real intrusions depend on many steps succeeding in sequence.

talks.title: Domains, Callbacks, Tokens and Exploits
talks.teaser: Traces a bug bounty hunt from an expired domain's callbacks to code execution in a Rancher-managed Kubernetes cluster.
talks.summary:
The talk follows a private bug bounty engagement against an unnamed company, told as a story from first discovery to payout. An automated scan flagged an unusual request to a subdomain. Checking the history showed the parent domain had expired, so the researcher re-registered it and set up wildcard DNS and a web server to record incoming requests. The callbacks carried bearer tokens and basic authentication headers tied to a Rancher Fleet agent.

The company first dismissed the finding as a forgotten development site, then asked the researcher to keep going. The researcher hypothesised that nodes did not re-check which management server they were talking to, so their workloads could be changed. Early attempts failed, and much time went into learning Rancher and Kubernetes and rebuilding the lab. Eventually the agent was pointed at a new server, scripts rewrote URLs and tokens on the fly, and command execution on real nodes followed. The containers reached internal networks, and a root mount of the host filesystem showed how loose the container security settings were.

The closing part covers the bounty and the lessons drawn. Persistence, careful documentation and not assuming which software is calling home all mattered. For defenders, expired domains that still point at old services, rapid response to alerts, and separating development from production networks stand out. The speaker also argues that clear two-way communication between triagers and researchers gives both sides a better outcome.

talks.title: Zero Trust - Dope or Nope
talks.teaser: Walks through zero trust principles, from MFA and RDP hardening to removing admin rights and network segmentation.
talks.summary:
Sami Laiho opens by arguing that zero trust is a poorly named idea and is easier to sell by focusing on what it gives users than on distrust. He frames it around three principles: verify explicitly, use least privilege, and assume breach. He stresses incremental adoption, since chasing a perfect deployment can leave an organisation with no protection at all.

The middle of the talk covers practical controls. He argues for MFA on internal networks as well as external ones, notes that a Windows PIN tied to the TPM counts as a factor, and recommends requiring MFA for RDP. He describes removing local admin rights as the most useful step, citing lower service desk ticket volumes and fewer reimaging jobs in customer examples, and points to privileged access management tools as a way to elevate specific applications. He also covers network micro-segmentation with IPsec and identity-based firewall rules.

To close, he demonstrates a home network built on the same ideas, with a privileged workstation as the only path to internal systems and an approval flow for elevation. The live portion ran long and did not fully succeed. His takeaway is that the goal is to slow attackers down enough to detect and respond, not to stop them outright.

talks.title: A Two part Saga: Continuing the Journey of Hacking Malware C2s
talks.teaser: Shows how malware command-and-control panels can be assessed with ordinary web application testing, using several malware families as case studies.
talks.summary:
The talk looks at the command-and-control panels that malware operators use to manage infected machines, and at how a researcher can assess them with standard web application testing instead of reverse engineering. It opens with an overview of the malware-as-a-service market, covering vendors, buyers and the short lifetime of a typical C2 server, which pushes the work toward automation and monitoring for newly appearing panels.

The middle section walks through a series of case studies. A stealer whose source had leaked was reached through a weakly protected archive and a user-controlled parameter that allowed a reverse shell upload. A dropper panel was opened by bypassing a file-name check and a PHP size-check function, while a phishing kit's login redirect was sidestepped by changing a response code. Other panels exposed default credentials, root passwords reused across many servers, and an enumerable task interface for a loader linked to ransomware groups, where archived development environments indicated that affected companies had been compromised.

The closing part discusses the legal and ethical grey areas of probing criminal infrastructure, the notification efforts toward affected organisations, and plans to continue this research. The takeaway for practitioners is that many malware backends are fragile web applications, and that disciplined web testing combined with automated monitoring can expose large numbers of compromised devices and give defenders useful leads.

talks.title: All Your Frontend Are Belong To Us - Crawling Through Javascript Using ASTs
talks.teaser: Shows how static analysis of JavaScript syntax trees can recover API endpoints and their arguments from minified frontend code.
talks.summary:
The talk looks at reconnaissance of web applications by pulling apart their frontend JavaScript. The speaker compares this to scouting in strategy games: map what is exposed, find hidden endpoints, and predict how the target is built before acting. Frontend bundles mix application code, library code and sometimes abandoned endpoints, and minification makes them hard to read with text matching.

The core idea is to parse the code into an abstract syntax tree rather than search for strings. Borrowing a habit from debugging, the approach starts at a fetch call and walks backwards to see where each argument comes from. It follows imports across files and renamed exports, then lists every way an endpoint is called. Because the tree stays the same when code is minified or its names change, the analysis holds up on production bundles. Browser native APIs are emulated, and common libraries are treated as wrappers around fetch or XMLHttpRequest.

The prototype, named Lurker, is still private and was shown on simple test code with some real results. Dynamic values remain the main burden, along with other pitfalls the speaker is still working through. The talk closes by asking for real applications to test against. The practical takeaway is that syntax-tree analysis can recover API surface from modern JavaScript more reliably than text search.

talks.title: Exploring Generative AI’s Threat to Social Justice and Democracy
talks.teaser: Explores how generative AI and personal data profiling threaten fairness, elections, hiring, and public institutions.
talks.summary:
The talk starts from the idea that personal data is being assembled into "digital twins," detailed profiles of individuals built from purchases, records and everyday interactions. The speakers trace how advertising moved from broadcast messages to demographic and psychographic targeting, then explain at a high level how generative models produce text one word at a time, with biases that are hard to predict or control.

The middle section surveys where these risks already appear. Schools are adopting generative tools faster than rules can follow, hiring platforms screen applicants with opaque models, and healthcare and predictive policing systems reproduce bias found in historical data. The speakers revisit political microtargeting, including the Cambridge Analytica case, and point to deepfake abuse that disproportionately pushes women and minorities out of public life.

The closing part argues that current regulation is late and weak on consent, and that it does not account for the lasting value of data already used to train models. The speakers urge the security community to demonstrate how these systems work, educate friends and family, and engage with policymakers, suggesting that durable protections may need to reach constitutional principles.

talks.title: Wi-Fi Roaming Security and Privacy
talks.teaser: Examines security and privacy issues in how Wi-Fi devices roam between access points.

talks.title: EU Hype Decoded CISCO MindX2 Crystal Ball Insights and CFA!
talks.teaser: Decodes the hype around EU cybersecurity developments and offers forward-looking insights on what comes next.

talks.title: I Was Almost a Cybercriminal
talks.teaser: Traces how a teen's app vulnerability report turned into a security career, and what steers young hackers away from crime.
talks.summary:
The talk asks why some young people drift into cybercrime and how communities, parents and companies can steer them elsewhere. The speaker belongs to Test Sér, a Finnish community where young people practise hacking and programming as a legal hobby. Working with a national cybercrime prevention campaign, the group surveyed 36 members. Responses pointed to parents, video games and game modding as common entry points, and showed that members were far from the lonely-nerd stereotype. Reasons for misbehaviour clustered around the appeal of forbidden activity, showing off to peers, a belief in anonymity and victimless crime, and the lure of free perks.

The central story is the speaker's own. As a teenager, they found that a mobile app's compiled JavaScript could be edited to bypass its activation check, unlocking free in-app rewards. They reported the flaw by email, were thanked with a small reward, and the vendor fixed it. The talk contrasts that outcome with punishment, which the speaker argues could easily have pushed them toward crime.

Practical advice follows for each audience. Parents are encouraged to redirect a child's skills toward bug bounties, capture-the-flag events and their own example. Companies should accept reports graciously, reward finders, publish a security.txt contact file and run training programmes to ease the skills shortage. Young people are pointed to communities, online learning resources and mental health support. Survey respondents also said they wanted clearer guidance on legal boundaries and easier ways to report issues.

talks.title: Securing GenAI? How Far Will Devsecops Take You and How to Go Further
talks.teaser: Maps DevSecOps and MLOps practices onto generative AI systems and argues that securing them needs a cross-disciplinary team.
talks.summary:
The talk opens with the speaker's move from data research into machine learning and AI security, and with a recurring problem: proofs of concept that never reach production. Machine learning engineers often come from research or data backgrounds and may lack grounding in DevOps, version control, testing and security, while security and infrastructure staff are rarely involved when models are built. Generative AI sharpens this, because a model can be wired into a product with a single API call and then behave in surprising ways without raising any error.

The middle section surveys the generative AI landscape and its failure modes. It describes retrieval-augmented generation as a common pattern for grounding a model in company data, explains that language models predict likely next tokens rather than check facts, and cites cases where a chatbot gave wrong advice with legal consequences. The threat list covers data and supply chain poisoning, prompt injection that gets around guardrails, leakage of private or company data, and denial-of-wallet attacks where every query costs money. The speaker also summarises a threat matrix that the team built.

The closing part argues for layering practices that already exist: backups, access control, encryption and updates, shared platform templates, and security checks at every stage rather than only before release. It also recommends human review of inputs and outputs, careful handling of personal data, and planning for how a model will be retired. The main takeaway is that no single person can cover machine learning, DevOps and security, so teams should bring those skills together from the start.

talks.title: Purple Teaming In Action: Beyond the Hype
talks.teaser: Shows how collaborative purple teaming tests EDR, Active Directory and evasion gaps, then turns findings into fixes.
talks.summary:
Tuomo Makkonen opens by defining purple teaming as a collaborative approach in which red and blue teams work together rather than against each other. He contrasts it with penetration testing and classic red teaming, which often end in a report with little shared visibility. Purple teaming runs open-book: scope, emulated adversaries and test cases are shared up front, then monthly iterations lead to joint review, mitigation and retesting.

The middle of the talk covers two areas in depth. The first is endpoint detection and response: how EDR agents collect telemetry, why raw alerts need context, and how evasion methods such as vulnerable-driver abuse, telemetry blocking and living-off-the-land techniques probe gaps in coverage. The second is on-premises Active Directory, covering certificate services, SCCM, exposed service-account credentials and attack paths mapped with BloodHound. Throughout, he argues for layered detection that combines brittle indicators with robust behavioural rules.

He closes with a getting-started sequence: set objectives, define scope, assemble stakeholders, use existing tools, secure executive support and iterate. Common pitfalls include chasing framework coverage for its own sake and red teams hiding from blue teams. He ends with predictions about cloud, APIs, supply chains and faster attacks, urging teams to stay grounded and learn from the past.

talks.title: Avoid Broken ACLs in Control Planes With Declarative RBAC
talks.teaser: Explains relationship-based access control as a way to avoid broken authorization in API servers and control planes.
talks.summary:
The talk opens with a common problem in building secure platforms: authorization checks are often hand-written conditionals scattered across an API server, which become hard to test and reason about as policies grow. Broken access control sits near the top of the OWASP API risks, and organisations that run many services with incompatible permission models struggle to see who can reach what.

The speaker compares offline token-based checks with centralized lookups, weighing revocation, consistency, availability and caching. Policy engines such as OPA and Cedar suit payload-driven decisions but struggle with reverse queries about who can access a resource. Relationship-based access control is then presented as a graph where permissions are paths between user and resource nodes, defined by a small schema. Worked examples cover team membership, role inheritance across folders and documents, and attribute combinations such as region and environment, all expressed in one graph. Published SpiceDB load figures are used to argue the model scales to very large edge counts.

The closing section sketches a control plane request flow, with authentication, flow control, authorization against a relationship store, admission, and filtered list responses, plus a controller that imports existing permissions into the graph. The practical takeaways are to separate policy decisions from application code, to test policies for equality and regression before rollout, to avoid letting users grant access they do not hold, and to build on existing open-source engines such as SpiceDB or OpenFGA instead of writing a graph engine from scratch.

talks.title: Integral Theory For Hackers
talks.teaser: Applies Ken Wilber's integral theory as a thinking lens for hacking, using Wi-Fi and BitLocker examples.
talks.summary:
The talk introduces integral theory, a multi-perspective framework linked to Ken Wilber that is common in management and psychology but rarely discussed in the hacker community. The speaker presents it as a possible thinking tool rather than a complete answer, and cautions against the hype that often surrounds new technologies. The core ideas are sketched out: holons, nested levels running from physical matter through minds, organizations and societies, and the four quadrants covering individual and collective perspectives, each seen from inside and outside.

To test the lens on security, the speaker walks through two public examples. The first is retrieving clear-text Wi-Fi passwords on Windows with a built-in netsh command, and how avoiding endpoint detection changes the approach. The second is a BitLocker bypass that relies on unencrypted communication with the TPM and a cheap logic analyzer sniffer, shown as a path that users and defenders tend to follow as they learn a platform. Each case is mapped onto the quadrants, covering the attacker's own reasoning, the tools and artifacts that get published, group norms, and broader legislation.

The closing argument is that new technology rarely changes everything, and that practitioners benefit from looking at history, psychology and other disciplines, both inward and across fields. The talk is deliberately demo-free and ends with a light joke about discovering that hacking one's own consciousness is the real target.

talks.title: Building Automated System for Deploying Lots of SA Systems for When SHTF
talks.teaser: Describes how a volunteer team automates cloud deployments and certificate-based user enrollment for a situational awareness server.
talks.summary:
The talk describes a volunteer project in Finland that builds an automated system for quickly deploying situational awareness tools, using the TAK server as the example product. The speakers explain how the plan shifted during development. An early Kubernetes approach on Azure Kubernetes Service did not work for a small volunteer team, and a network load balancer that could not handle TCP and UDP on the same port blocked one product. The team moved to virtual machines, then to Azure Container Apps as it matured, and used Pulumi to manage infrastructure state in place of an older Terraform pipeline.

The middle of the talk covers the enrollment design. An internal certificate authority service, built on CFSSL behind a Python API, issues mutual TLS certificates. Each deployment gets a single-use administrator login, and new users are approved by an administrator who checks a validation code after scanning a QR code. Revocation is handled centrally, because the products do not manage their own enrollment. The speakers also outline the state of the official TAK client builds and how packages were rebuilt from public releases. A live demo let attendees try enrollment during the session, and at least one person completed the flow.

The closing section focuses on the project's needs. It runs on volunteer time with a small number of key people, so it is at risk if those people leave. The speakers listed missing roles: integration developers, DevOps engineers, QA and test specialists, PKI experts, and frontend and UX designers. They noted that a professional UX designer made the enrollment flow much easier to use, and that testing coverage is still thin outside the core API.

talks.title: Cybersecurity in the Gaming Industry
talks.teaser: Surveys cyber threats facing game companies, from DDoS and account takeovers to regulatory standards and secure development practice.
talks.summary:
The talk opens by explaining why security matters so much in the games industry. The speaker names three main assets at stake: money moving through game platforms, players' personal data, and intellectual property such as unreleased titles. He stresses that players, developers and publishers each share responsibility, and that training and awareness are the most effective defence.

The middle section surveys the threats and the games most exposed to them. Massively multiplayer and competitive online titles draw DDoS attacks and cheating, while mobile and free-to-play games often lack strong protection. Cross-platform titles are hard to secure consistently, and legacy servers and game development tools can hide serious weaknesses. Phishing, account takeover, ransomware on game databases, insider leaks and fraud complete the list, with attacks rising sharply during the pandemic.

For the close, he recommends that studios adopt a recognised framework and map the regulations that apply, such as GDPR and payment card rules, since breaches can carry heavy fines. He suggests a security architecture reference model covering data, applications, endpoints, networks and cloud, backed by a secure development lifecycle and an incident response plan. His practical advice is to scan environments, run penetration tests regularly and act on findings through a remediation plan.

talks.title: The Rising Flame of Community Engagement
talks.teaser: Explains how trust turns loose professional networks into communities, using a Nordic financial sharing group and Women for Cyber as examples.
talks.summary:
The talk opens with a question: what separates a community from a network? The speaker describes a network as a looser, more transactional set of relationships where people mostly receive, while a community asks members to contribute, take part and share a sense of belonging and a common purpose. Drawing on social psychology, the talk argues that trust is the foundation that lets that sense of community form, because members accept vulnerability on the expectation that others will not exploit it.

The middle section tests this with two case studies. The first is a cross-border partnership of Nordic financial institutions, founded in 2017, where competing banks agree not to compete on cyber defence. Members share threat intelligence, support one another during incidents and bring in public bodies and law enforcement, which gives smaller firms with thin security teams access to insight and tools they could not afford alone. The second is Women for Cyber, a European network that aims to diversify the field through upskilling and by correcting misconceptions about cyber careers. The speaker frames the benefits of such communities as reciprocation, having a trusted sparring partner, a sense of belonging, and time to reflect and learn after a crisis.

The closing advice is practical. Individuals should join a local community even before they can contribute much, and start one if none exists. Organisations, particularly small and mid-sized ones, should build on relationships they already have, make a business case around shared interests and cost savings, and take the initiative rather than wait for others to drive collaboration.

talks.title: Identifying Cross-Account Attack Paths in AWS Environments at Scale
talks.teaser: Shows how cross-account IAM role assumption creates attack paths in large AWS organizations, and how a graph tool maps them.
talks.summary:
The talk starts from the problem that AWS resources live inside accounts, which act as security boundaries, while IAM roles can be assumed across accounts through trust policies and permissions. Chaining these assumptions lets an identity move step by step through an organization. The speaker notes that most AWS security incidents trace back to IAM, and that in environments with hundreds of accounts and thousands of roles, checking every possible assumption path by hand is impractical.

The middle of the talk reviews existing open-source options. Cartography maps resources but works only within a single account, so it misses cross-account trust. The speaker's team built IAM Graph, which takes account authorization data collected from each account, loads it into a Neo4j graph, and uses IAM Speculator-style evaluation via IAM Spy, an SMT-solver-based engine, to confirm which principals can actually assume which roles. A recorded demo showed a user in one account reaching an admin role in another account through a chain of roles.

The conclusion is that the tool has been run in environments with hundreds of accounts, where analysis takes time but works. Its purpose is to reveal unnecessary cross-account access and overly broad trust policies so they can be removed. It is not a full IAM audit tool and does not yet check for excessive permissions or privilege escalation. Future ideas include enriching the graph with data about sensitive accounts and adding queries for interesting paths. At the time, the tool was not yet public, with plans to open-source it and IAM Spy soon.

talks.title: Have U Been Invited (episode 2) - MacOS Logic Bugs
talks.teaser: Walks through a zero-click macOS calendar exploit chain that escapes the sandbox, evades Gatekeeper and reaches protected photos.
talks.summary:
This talk is a follow-up to last year's presentation on a macOS Calendar vulnerability. The earlier flaw allowed an arbitrary file write through attachment file names in calendar events. Fixes were still pending at the time, so the full chain could not be shown then. This episode picks up from that point and walks through the chain step by step, starting from a write that is confined to the Calendar app's sandbox.

The middle of the talk covers each obstacle in turn. The write is used to plant a local calendar, which can carry alert actions, and a legacy migration marker that forces the app to index it. A disk image is then planted so that Finder mounts a remote share and indexes an application inside it, which avoids the quarantine flag that Gatekeeper checks. A newly registered URL handler launches that application, which runs code and changes the Photos library configuration. Photos then syncs the user's iCloud library into a directory the attacker controls, so the protected original folder is never accessed directly.

The closing section reviews the disclosure timeline, which ran from late 2022 into late 2023 with several rounds of back-and-forth with Apple over CVE assignment and credit. The practical takeaway is that small logic errors in file handling, combined with hidden app features and configuration, can get around several macOS protections at once.

talks.title: CERT and NCSC 101
talks.teaser: Walks through how national CERTs and NCSCs work, from incident triage to international information sharing.
talks.summary:
The talk opens with how computer emergency response teams emerged after the 1988 Morris worm and spread into hundreds of teams worldwide. It separates a CERT from a security operations centre: a CERT serves a defined constituency and shares information rather than running an organisation's own defences. The speaker then walks through how a national team triages incoming reports and sends notice-and-takedown requests to hosting providers and network operators.

Case studies form the middle. Traffic data from a 2007 wave of attacks on Estonia let teams ask many countries to clean up compromised machines. A criminal hosting provider that kept receiving fresh address blocks showed why takedowns alone fail. During a 2016 botnet that exploited home routers, automated reports led to a coordinated warning to operators and users. Groups such as FIRST and the EGC provide channels for this work, each with different levels of trust.

The closing section covers the NIS2 directive, which writes national CERT duties into law and separates them from regulators so organisations feel safe reporting. The takeaway is to report incidents early, know who to call, and build relationships before a crisis hits.
